items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro: Benchmarks, Pricing and How to Use It
items.content:
Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI’s newest flagship model, and it lands less than a point behind Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at about a fifth of the output price. Moonshot calls it its “most capable 3T-class open-weight model”, and the full weights are due by 4 November 2026. In the video below I put it side by side with Claude on real builds. Here’s what it is, how it scores, what it costs and where it still falls short.

Key takeaways

- Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with far more post-training compute.

- 65.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 vs 66.4 for Opus 5.5 and 58.2 for GPT-6 Astra.

- API price: $2 in / $10 out per million tokens, with a 1M-token context.

- Open weights promised by 4 November 2026. Claim a free strategy session to plan your model stack.

## What is Kimi K3.1 Pro?

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the first model in Moonshot’s K3.1 series. According to the official Kimi blog, it isn’t a brand-new base model. It’s Kimi K3 with a much bigger post-training run on top. That’s where the gains come from: better long coding jobs, better tool use and fewer made-up claims.

Moonshot describes it as a “3T-class” open-weight model. It hasn’t published an exact parameter count for K3.1 Pro, so I won’t guess one. What we do know is the context window: 1 million tokens. That’s enough for a big codebase, a long contract pack or months of notes in one go.

There’s also a Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed variant. It’s the same model served faster — Moonshot says two to three times the speed — for twice the price.

## Kimi K3.1 Pro benchmarks

Here are the numbers Moonshot published. Remember these are the maker’s own results, so treat them as a starting point and test on your own work.

The headline is Terminal-Bench. That test checks whether a model can actually get work done in a terminal, step by step. K3.1 Pro sits 0.7 points behind Opus 5.5 and well ahead of GPT-6 Astra. On BenchCAD without tools it’s almost level with Opus 5.5 and well clear of Fable 5.1 (60.6).

On long coding jobs, Moonshot’s internal Kimi Code Bench 3.0 went from 55.95 on K3 to 61.2 on K3.1 Pro. Business work improved too: OfficeQA Pro v2 is 64.4, which Moonshot claims is the best score so far, and Frontier Finance is 58.6. The biggest jump was in an internal business-operations test, from 8.9 to 37.

The demo that stuck with me is the walking test. Moonshot gave it a human body model with 296 skeleton parts and 402 muscle parts. The walk went from collapsing straight away to 11.2 seconds of steady walking, after the model found and fixed 36 shoulder-muscle errors.

## Kimi K3.1 Pro pricing

This is where it gets interesting. Here are the prices from the Kimi API pricing page, per million tokens:

So K3.1 Pro is actually cheaper than K3 while scoring higher. Cache writes cost $2.00 for a 5-minute cache and $4.00 for a 1-hour cache. Caching is automatic, which helps a lot if you keep sending the same big codebase or system prompt.

One heads-up: the K2 series closes to new users on 31 October 2026 and retires at the end of December 2026. If you’re still on K2, now is a good time to move.

## Where you can use Kimi K3.1 Pro

- Kimi.ai on the web, plus the iOS, Android and HarmonyOS apps.

- Kimi Work desktop app, version 3.1.0 or later, on Windows and Apple silicon Macs.

- Kimi Code — switch with the /model command.

- The Kimi API as `kimi-k3.1-pro` and `kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed`, with zero data retention available.

- Business and Enterprise workspaces, where an admin has to switch it on first (it’s off by default).

The API is OpenAI-compatible, so most tools that talk to OpenAI can talk to Kimi by changing the base URL. You unlock it after a top-up of at least $1. If you want to run it inside Hermes Agent, I wrote a separate step-by-step guide: Kimi K3.1 Pro in Hermes.

Want the short version? I also wrote my Kimi K3.1 Pro breakdown on the AI Profit Boardroom blog.

## What I like about it

Three things stand out. First, the price-to-score ratio. Getting within a point of Opus 5.5 on terminal work for $10 per million output tokens is a big deal if you run agents all day. Second, the 1M context with automatic caching, which keeps long sessions cheap. Third, the open weights. Once they land, you can run it on your own hardware or with a host you trust.

It also works well for 3D and game work. Moonshot says it works with Unity, Unreal, Godot and Three.js scenes, and it powers the “3D Make” feature on kimi.ai.

## The limits you should know

It isn’t perfect, and Moonshot is upfront about that.

- Hallucinations: on Moonshot’s hard hallucination test with tools, K3.1 Pro made false claims at a rate of 8.3. That’s much better than K3 (23.4) and Opus 5.5 (15.0), but GPT-6 Astra was lower still at 5.5. Moonshot says this is a stress test, not a normal daily rate.

- Cyber security work: Moonshot says K3.1 Pro is behind the top closed models here, and it removed cyber data for the open-weight release.

- Web search tool: the API’s built-in search is being updated, and Moonshot doesn’t recommend it for production right now.

- Thinking is always on. You can lower the reasoning effort for speed, but you can’t switch thinking off.

Check facts in anything customer-facing. Lower hallucination rates are still not zero.

## Kimi K3.1 Pro vs Claude Opus 5.5

In my video I gave both models the same build tasks. Opus 5.5 still edges it on the hardest work, and the benchmarks agree. But the gap is small, and Kimi costs a fraction of the price. For most everyday agent jobs — coding, research, documents — I’d be happy running K3.1 Pro and keeping Opus for the hardest jobs.

## My verdict on Kimi K3.1 Pro

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the most capable open-weight model I’ve tested this month. It’s close to Opus 5.5 on terminal work, cheaper than the model it replaces, and open weights are on the way. If you run agents every day and watch your costs, Kimi K3.1 Pro deserves a spot in your stack.

Spark-X2.6-4B is a new 4B open model from the SparkLLM Team, and it scores well above its size on agent and coding tests. It has a 1M-token context window, three thinking levels and an Apache 2.0 licence. It came out a little over a month after Spark-X2.5-4B and uses the same architecture, so the gains come from better post-training. In the video below I test it on real jobs. Key takeaways

- 4B parameters, Apache 2.0, English and Chinese.

- Average benchmark score 63.3 vs 52.1 for Spark-X2.5-4B.

- 1M context, if your device has enough memory.

- Runs in Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM and MLX.

## What is Spark-X2.6-4B?

Spark-X2.6-4B is a small language model from the SparkLLM Team, published on Hugging Face under the XHToken organisation. The model card says it keeps the same architecture as Spark-X2.5-4B, with the improvement coming from post-training. There is also a base checkpoint, Spark-X2.6-4B-Base, if you want to fine-tune it.

items.content:
A Kimi K3.1 Pro Hermes setup is one of the cheapest ways to get near-Opus coding power inside your own AI agent. Hermes already has a built-in Kimi provider, so setup takes a few minutes. In this guide I’ll walk you through the API key, the exact commands, the one setting that controls your token bill, and how to save it as a reusable profile. The video below shows it running.

Key takeaways

- Hermes talks to Kimi through the built-in kimi-coding provider.

- Put your key in ~/.hermes/.env as `KIMI_API_KEY`.

- Watch reasoning effort: max uses about 3× the tokens of medium.

- Save it as a profile so one word starts a Kimi agent. Claim a free strategy session for help.

## Why run Kimi K3.1 Pro in Hermes?

Hermes Agent gives you memory, skills, scheduled jobs and tools. The model is the brain you plug in. Kimi K3.1 Pro is a strong brain for the money: Moonshot’s launch post puts it at 65.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, just behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4, and it costs $2 in and $10 out per million tokens.

That mix matters for agents. An agent might run for hours, read big files and call tools many times. A cheaper model that still finishes the job keeps those long runs affordable. And with a 1M-token context, Hermes can hold a lot of your project in view at once.

If you want the full model breakdown first — benchmarks, limits and pricing — read my Kimi K3.1 Pro review. This page is just about getting it running in Hermes.

## Step 1: Get your Kimi API key

- Go to the Kimi platform and create an API key.

- Top up at least $1. Moonshot’s quickstart says K3.1 Pro unlocks after a top-up, and your rate tier depends on how much you’ve topped up in total.

- Copy the key somewhere safe. Never paste it into a chat or commit it to GitHub.

If you’re in mainland China, Hermes has a separate provider called `kimi-coding-cn`, which uses `KIMI_CN_API_KEY` instead.

## Step 2: Add the key to Hermes

Hermes reads provider keys from its.env file. Add one line:

```
# ~/.hermes/.env
KIMI_API_KEY=your-key-here
```

By default Hermes sends Kimi requests to `https://api.moonshot.ai/v1`. You only need `KIMI_BASE_URL` if you want to point somewhere else. The full provider list is in the Hermes docs.

## Step 3: Start a chat with Kimi K3.1 Pro

Run this in your terminal:

```
hermes chat --provider kimi-coding --model kimi-k3.1-pro
```

That’s it. Give it a real task — fix a bug, build a page, summarise a folder of notes — and watch how it works through it. Want more speed? Swap in the Highspeed model:

```
hermes chat --provider kimi-coding --model kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed
```

Highspeed is two to three times faster but costs double: $4 in and $20 out per million tokens. I use the normal model for long background jobs and Highspeed when I’m sitting there waiting.

## Step 4: Control your token bill with reasoning effort

This is the setting most people miss. Kimi K3.1 Pro always thinks before it answers. You can’t switch thinking off, but you can choose how hard it thinks: low, high or max.

Setting
What happens
Use it for

Hermes default (medium)
Hermes sends medium if you don’t set anything
Everyday tasks

high
More thinking, more tokens
Tricky bugs, planning

max
Kimi’s own default; about 3× the tokens of medium
The hardest jobs only

low
Fastest replies
Quick edits, chat

To set it for every session, run this inside Hermes:

```
/reasoning high --global
```

Hermes saves that, so you don’t have to set it again. My advice: start on medium, and only move up when the model gets stuck. Max can triple your token use on the same task.

## Step 5: Make Kimi your default or save it as a profile

If you want Kimi every time, set it as the default model:

```
hermes config set model.provider kimi-coding
hermes config set model.default kimi-k3.1-pro
```

I prefer profiles. A profile is a separate Hermes setup with its own model, memory and skills. Make a coding profile that runs on Kimi:

```
hermes profile create coder
coder setup
coder chat
```

Now typing `coder chat` starts your Kimi coding agent, while your main Hermes keeps its own model and memory. You can also add short names in `model.aliases` so switching models mid-chat is quicker.

Step 5 Preview comes from StepFun. The Hugging Face model card calls it “StepFun’s flagship model for agentic work”. It is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 600B total parameters and 27B active per token, and it takes text and images as input.

I want to be clear here. In my video it was free to run inside Hermes at the time of recording. Check current pricing before you rely on that. I couldn’t find an official source that confirms a free window, which provider offers it or when it ends.

The official numbers are these. StepFun’s pricing page lists step-5-preview at $1.00 per million input tokens ($0.10 on a cache hit) and $2.70 per million output tokens. The Nous inference API listed stepfun/step-5-preview at the same paid price when we checked, with no free variant at that time.

The weights are open under the StepFun Model License 1.0, which StepFun describes as Apache-2.0-style with attribution and some commercial conditions. Device makers and model-as-a-service businesses with over $20M revenue over 12 months need a separate commercial licence. Internal use is exempt. For almost every small business, it works like a normal open licence.

You can self-host the weights with vLLM or SGLang (OpenAI-compatible) or Transformers. It is big: the FP8 build needs a 4×B300 node or an 8×H200 node. Recommended settings are temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 0. For most people the API route is far easier.

## Why GPT-6.1 Sol matters for coding

Most coding models are judged on Python and JavaScript. OpenAI tried something harder: old languages that very few people still write. On 19 October 2026 it shared results on COBOL, the language still behind a huge amount of banking.

OpenAI’s own figures show why that matters. COBOL supports over 40% of online banking, 80% of in-person card payments and 95% of ATM transactions. Moving that code to something modern is slow and risky, and the people who know COBOL are retiring.

If you want the full model overview first — pricing, availability and non-coding benchmarks — read my GPT-6.1 Sol guide.

Here’s how the test worked. The model had to move a COBOL program to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python or Rust. Hidden tests then checked that the new program gave exactly the same outputs, byte for byte. A task only counted if every test passed.

OpenAI’s Codex model guide says to use GPT-6.1 Sol for complex coding and agent work when your account has it. Here are the commands:

```
# start Codex on GPT-6.1 Sol
codex --model gpt-6.1-sol

# one-off job without opening a session
codex exec -m gpt-6.1-sol "Review the current changes"
```

To make it your default, add one line to your Codex config.toml:

```
model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
```

Inside a session, type `/model` to switch models or change the effort level. It works in the Codex desktop app and the CLI.

Codex names the effort levels from Light to Ultra. Light is the same as Low in the CLI.

OpenAI’s own advice is that most tasks don’t need Max or Ultra. I agree. Start on Medium and move up only if it gets stuck.

- Run your own test suite, not just the model’s.

- Ship in small pieces you can roll back.

items.content:
A DeepSeek V4.1 Flash OpenCode setup is one of the easiest ways to get a strong AI coding agent for free right now. OpenCode Zen lists a free DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model for a limited time, so you can start without an API key. In the video below I set it up and build with it. This guide gives you the install commands, the free and paid routes, and how to use Plan, Build and subagents.

Key takeaways

- OpenCode Zen has a free deepseek-v4.1-flash-free model for a limited time.

- Install with one command, then pick the model with `/models`.

- Or use your own DeepSeek key via `/connect`.

- Use Plan first, then Build. Claim a free strategy session for help.

## Why DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and OpenCode?

OpenCode is an open-source coding agent that runs in your terminal. It reads your project, makes changes and runs commands. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is a fast, cheap model with strong coding scores: after the 17 October update it hits 77.0 on DeepSWE, per its model card.

Put them together and you get a capable coding agent that costs nothing while the free offer lasts. If you want the model details — architecture, pricing and benchmarks — read my DeepSeek V4.1 Flash guide. This page is the hands-on setup.

## Step 1: Install OpenCode

Pick one of these, from the OpenCode docs:

```
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash

# or with npm
npm install -g opencode-ai

# or with Homebrew
brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode
```

Be careful with Homebrew: `brew install opencode` installs OpenCode 2, which is a different package. Use the tap command above. Then open your project folder and run:

```
opencode
```

## Step 2: Pick the free DeepSeek model

OpenCode Zen is OpenCode’s own set of hosted models. The Zen docs list deepseek-v4.1-flash-free as “Free for a limited time”.

- Type `/models` inside OpenCode.

- Choose DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free.

- Zen model IDs look like `opencode/<model-id>` if you set it in config.

Zen says the free model uses zero data retention and isn’t used for training. Free chat models only work inside OpenCode. If you don’t want to see free models at all, set `OPENCODE_DISABLE_FREE_MODELS=1`.

Free offers end. When this one does, switch to the paid Zen model or your own DeepSeek key below.

## Step 3 (optional): Use your own DeepSeek key

Want more control or higher limits? Connect DeepSeek directly, as the providers page explains:

- Type `/connect` in OpenCode.

- Choose DeepSeek and paste your API key.

- Run `/models` and pick the DeepSeek model.

OpenCode saves your key in `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`. Run `opencode auth list` to see which providers you’ve connected.

## Step 4: Set up your project with /init

Run `/init` the first time you open a project. OpenCode reads your code and writes an AGENTS.md file. That file tells the agent how your project is laid out, how to run it and what rules to follow. Commit it so every session starts with the same context.

Use `@` to find and attach files to your message, and `/undo` or `/redo` if a change goes wrong.

## Step 5: Plan first, then Build

OpenCode has two main modes. Press Tab to switch between them.

Mode
What it does
When to use it

Plan
Thinks through the job without editing files
Start every bigger task here

Build
Edits files and runs commands
Once you’re happy with the plan

This is the habit that saves the most time. Ask for a plan, read it, fix anything that’s wrong, then switch to Build. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is fast, so this loop feels quick.

## Step 6: Use subagents for bigger jobs

OpenCode comes with two subagents, General and Explore. Mention one with `@general` to hand it a side task, like searching the codebase, while your main agent keeps working. Per the agents docs, subagents use the same model as the agent that called them, so they’ll run on DeepSeek too.

You can also make your own agents:

```
opencode agent create
opencode agent list
```

Custom agents live in `.opencode/agents/` in your project or `~/.config/opencode/agents/` for all projects. Each one has a short header with its description, mode, model and permissions.

- A small landing page from a one-paragraph brief.

- A script that tidies a messy folder of files.

- Tests for an existing function you don’t trust.

- A bug fix, with Plan mode explaining the cause first.

Start small, check the output, then give it bigger jobs. Always review changes before you push them.

It has a 1M-token context, open MIT weights and output pricing as low as $0.60 per million tokens off-peak. In the video below I run it free inside OpenCode. - Open weights under the MIT licence. Claim a free strategy session to plan your stack.

## What is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash?

DeepSeek launched V4.1 Flash on 10 September 2026. It’s a 552-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, but only a small part runs for each token: 8B active when reading input and 16B when writing output. That’s why it’s fast and cheap.

It also uses a new design DeepSeek calls a Causal Encoder-Decoder. The model card lists 40 layers (20 encoder and 20 decoder) and 384 routed experts plus one shared expert, with six active at a time. The practical win is memory: its KV cache needs about a quarter of the GPU memory of the previous generation.

- The API name is deepseek-flash, which now points at V4.1-Flash-1017.

- Since 14 September, `deepseek-v4-pro` requests also go to V4.1 Flash at Flash prices until V4.1 Pro launches.

- It supports thinking (the default) and non-thinking modes, JSON output, tool calls, the Responses API and the Anthropic API format.

The Anthropic-format support is handy. Tools built for Claude can often point at DeepSeek with only a base URL and key change.

## How to run DeepSeek V4.1 Flash

You have three main options:

- The DeepSeek API: easiest, and cheap off-peak.

- Your own hardware: the 1017 weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope. Serve them with vLLM, SGLang or Docker Model Runner. Community quantisations exist for llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio.

- OpenCode: a free version is available there for a limited time. I wrote a full walkthrough: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in OpenCode.

```
docker model run hf.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017
```

DeepSeek recommends temperature 1.0, top_p 1.0 and a max token budget of at least 256K for hard tasks.

Want the short version? I also wrote my DeepSeek V4.1 Flash summary on the AI Profit Boardroom blog.

## Who should use it?

If you run lots of agent jobs and want them cheap, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is hard to beat. It’s great for coding agents, automation and long documents. If you need the very best terminal performance, a top closed model still leads. And as with any model, check its work on anything that matters.

## Tips to keep DeepSeek costs down

- Run batch jobs off-peak. Everything outside the peak windows is half price.

- Reuse the same prompt start. Cache hits cost $0.006 per million tokens at peak, against $0.30 for a miss.

- Use non-thinking mode for simple jobs like formatting or short replies.

- Cap output length. Max output is 384K tokens, so set a sensible limit for everyday jobs.

Done right, a whole day of agent work can cost less than a coffee. Just check the bill after your first week so there are no surprises.

Self-hosting is another option once your volume is high. The weights are free under MIT, and with only 16B active parameters per output token it’s far lighter to serve than its 552B size suggests. You still need serious GPU memory for the full model, so most people should start on the API.

DeepSeek’s fast, low-cost model: a 552B mixture-of-experts with 8B active for input and 16B for output, a 1M-token context and open MIT weights.

What changed in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017?

The 17 October update raised benchmark scores, finished tasks faster and wrote shorter answers. Terminal-Bench 4.0 went from 31.2 to 42.3.

How much does DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cost?

$0.30 input and $1.20 output per million tokens at peak, and half that off-peak. Cached input is $0.006 at peak.

Is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash open source?

Yes. The weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope under the MIT licence.

What is the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash API model name?

deepseek-flash. The old deepseek-v4-flash names route to it.
